claim: Chronic hypoxia (7% O2 for 28 days) induced cognitive dysfunction in mice, as evidenced by significantly decreased alternation behavior in Y-maze tests.
source: The results of the Y-maze tests showed that the alternation behavior was significantly decreased, and the novel object recognition tests showed that the exploration time of new objects was significantly reduced after hypoxia, suggesting that hypoxia induced cognitive dysfunction in mice (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral test data (Y-maze) presented in Figure 1B showing statistical significance.

claim: Chronic hypoxia (7% O2 for 28 days) reduced exploration time of new objects in novel object recognition tests in mice.
source: The results of the Y-maze tests showed that the alternation behavior was significantly decreased, and the novel object recognition tests showed that the exploration time of new objects was significantly reduced after hypoxia, suggesting that hypoxia induced cognitive dysfunction in mice (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral test data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: Chronic hypoxia (7% O2 for 28 days) significantly reduced movement distance in open-field tests in mice.
source: Assuming that the total exercise times were similar in both groups, the exercise distance and speed were also significantly reduced in H28d mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by open-field test data showing reduced movement distance in Figure 1E.

claim: Chronic hypoxia (7% O2 for 28 days) significantly reduced movement speed in open-field tests in mice.
source: Assuming that the total exercise times were similar in both groups, the exercise distance and speed were also significantly reduced in H28d mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by open-field test data showing reduced movement speed in Figure 1E.

claim: Chronic hypoxia (7% O2 for 28 days) induced motor function impairment in mice.
source: Assuming that the total exercise times were similar in both groups, the exercise distance and speed were also significantly reduced in H28d mice (Figure 1E). These results suggested that the motor function was impaired after hypoxia.
evidence: Inferred from reduced movement distance and speed in open-field tests.

claim: Chronic hypoxia (7% O2 for 28 days) induced anxiety-like behavior in mice, as evidenced by reduced time exploring the central area of the open field.
source: In addition, H28d mice spent less time exploring the central area of the open field and crossing the central area, indicating anxiety-like behavior (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by open-field test data showing reduced central area exploration in Figure 1F.

claim: Chronic hypoxia (7% O2 for 28 days) caused disordered neuronal arrangement in the hippocampal CA1 region with gaps, abnormal arrangement, and darker cytoplasm.
source: Nissl staining showed that neurons in the hippocampal CA1 region were disordered in H28d group, with gaps, abnormal arrangement, and darker cytoplasm compared with Con group, suggesting that the hippocampus was damaged in H28d group (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by Nissl staining data presented in Figure 1G.

claim: Chronic hypoxia (7% O2 for 28 days) caused hippocampal damage in mice.
source: Nissl staining showed that neurons in the hippocampal CA1 region were disordered in H28d group, with gaps, abnormal arrangement, and darker cytoplasm compared with Con group, suggesting that the hippocampus was damaged in H28d group (Figure 1G).
evidence: Inferred from Nissl staining showing neuronal disorganization.

claim: Chronic hypoxia (7% O2 for 28 days) caused obvious atrophy of the hippocampal region in mice.
source: It was also found that the hippocampal region of H28d group showed obvious atrophy (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by hippocampal area measurements presented in Figure 1H.

claim: Chronic hypoxia (7% O2 for 28 days) induced neurodegeneration in the cerebral cortex and hippocampal region in mice.
source: Neuronal degeneration staining (Fluoro-Jade B [FJB] staining) showed neurodegeneration in the cerebral cortex and hippocampal region in mice in H28d group (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by FJB staining data presented in Figure 1I.

claim: Chronic hypoxia (7% O2 for 28 days) significantly reduced the density of dendritic spines on neurons in the hippocampus.
source: We also carried out Golgi staining to reveal the morphology and structure of neurons in the brains in the two groups of mice and showed that the density of dendritic spines on neurons was significantly lower in H28d group (Figure 1J and K).
evidence: Supported by Golgi staining data and quantification presented in Figure 1J and K.

claim: Chronic hypoxia induced cognitive and motor dysfunction and nerve damage in mice.
source: Above all, chronic hypoxia induced cognitive and motor dysfunction and nerve damage in mice.
evidence: Summary statement based on multiple behavioral and histological findings presented in the study.

claim: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing identified 13 cell types in mouse brain tissue.
source: To explore the molecular mechanism responsible for chronic hypoxia-induced nerve injury in the brain, we performed snRNA-seq of two groups and visualized the distribution of gene expression in all samples using UMAP visualization and identified 13 cell types according to the expression of cell-specific markers (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by snRNA-seq data and UMAP visualization in Figure 2A.

claim: Endothelial cells had the highest number of differentially expressed genes after hypoxia, and most of them were upregulated.
source: Among these, the number of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) in endothelial cells (ECs) was the highest after hypoxia, and most of them were upregulated (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by DEG analysis presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The mRNA expression levels of hemoglobin subunits (Hba-a1, Hba-a2, Hbb-bs, Hbb-bt) were significantly upregulated in most non-neuronal cells after hypoxia.
source: We subsequently displayed DEGs in all cell subsets, labeled the top 10 genes, and found the mRNA expression levels of hemoglobin subunits (Hba-a1, Hba-a2, Hbb-bs, Hbb-bt) were significantly upregulated in most non-neuronal cells after hypoxia, indicating that might be a common mechanism whereby various non-neuronal cells in the brain respond to hypoxic stress (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by DEG analysis showing hemoglobin upregulation in Figure 2D.

claim: Upregulation of hemoglobin subunits in non-neuronal cells might be a common mechanism whereby various non-neuronal cells in the brain respond to hypoxic stress.
source: We subsequently displayed DEGs in all cell subsets, labeled the top 10 genes, and found the mRNA expression levels of hemoglobin subunits (Hba-a1, Hba-a2, Hbb-bs, Hbb-bt) were significantly upregulated in most non-neuronal cells after hypoxia, indicating that might be a common mechanism whereby various non-neuronal cells in the brain respond to hypoxic stress (Figure 2D).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that hemoglobin is upregulated across multiple non-neuronal cell types.

claim: The number and intensity of intercellular communications in the brain both increased after hypoxia.
source: We found that the number and intensity of intercellular communications in the brain both increased after hypoxia.
evidence: Supported by CellChat analysis presented in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Various non-neuronal cells in the brain jointly transcribed hemoglobin under chronic hypoxic stress, which might represent a common mechanism in response to hypoxic stress.
source: Above all, these results suggested that various non-neuronal cells in the brain jointly transcribed hemoglobin under chronic hypoxic stress, which might represent a common mechanism in response to hypoxic stress.
evidence: Summary statement based on snRNA-seq findings showing hemoglobin upregulation across multiple cell types.

claim: Hypoxia is an important factor inducing EVs release by cells.
source: Hypoxia has been shown to be an important factor inducing EVs release by cells, suggesting that the EVs-mediated communication pathway may be an important mechanism for cells to respond to hypoxia (Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2023.

claim: EVs-mediated communication pathway may be an important mechanism for cells to respond to hypoxia.
source: Hypoxia has been shown to be an important factor inducing EVs release by cells, suggesting that the EVs-mediated communication pathway may be an important mechanism for cells to respond to hypoxia (Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that hypoxia induces EV release, as cited from Wang et al., 2023.

claim: EVs isolated from mouse brain tissue have a diameter of approximately 100 nm and display a characteristic cup-shaped morphology.
source: Transmission electron microscopy confirmed that the diameter of the EVs was approximately 100 nm and displayed a characteristic cup-shaped morphology (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy data in Figure 3B.

claim: EVs isolated from mouse brain tissue show positive expression of EV markers TSG101, HSP90, and CD9.
source: Western blot analysis revealed positive expression of EV markers TSG101, HSP90, and CD9, while calnexin was not detected (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 3C.

claim: Calnexin was not detected in EVs isolated from mouse brain tissue.
source: Western blot analysis revealed positive expression of EV markers TSG101, HSP90, and CD9, while calnexin was not detected (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 3C showing absence of calnexin.

claim: The predominant size of isolated EVs from mouse brain tissue ranged from 50 to 200 nm.
source: Nanoparticle tracking analysis indicated that the predominant size of the isolated EVs ranged from 50 to 200 nm, with increased EV secretion observed in the brains following hypoxia (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by nanoparticle tracking analysis data in Figure 3D.

claim: Increased EV secretion was observed in the brains following hypoxia.
source: Nanoparticle tracking analysis indicated that the predominant size of the isolated EVs ranged from 50 to 200 nm, with increased EV secretion observed in the brains following hypoxia (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by nanoparticle tracking analysis data in Figure 3D.

claim: A total of 2257 differentially expressed genes were identified in EVs between control and hypoxia groups, of which 1493 were upregulated and 764 were downregulated after hypoxia.
source: A total of 2257 DEGs were identified, of which 1493 were upregulated and 764 were downregulated after hypoxia.
evidence: Supported by EVs-RNA-seq analysis.

claim: Hemoglobin mRNA was significantly upregulated in EVs after hypoxia.
source: Hemoglobin mRNA was also significantly upregulated in EVs after hypoxia, consistent with the snRNA-seq results (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by EVs-RNA-seq data presented in Figure 3E.

claim: Several pathways related to RNA metabolism were significantly upregulated in EVs after hypoxia.
source: We found that several pathways related to RNA metabolism were significantly upregulated, while several pathways associated with energy metabolism were downregulated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F, Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by gene enrichment analysis of EVs-RNA-seq data.

claim: Several pathways associated with energy metabolism were downregulated in EVs after hypoxia.
source: We found that several pathways related to RNA metabolism were significantly upregulated, while several pathways associated with energy metabolism were downregulated (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–F, Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by gene enrichment analysis of EVs-RNA-seq data.

claim: Energy metabolism pathways in the brain may have been damaged by hypoxia.
source: These results suggested that energy metabolism pathways in the brain may have been damaged by hypoxia, and various cell types in the brain may regulate RNA metabolism via the EVs pathway to resist hypoxic injury.
evidence: Inferred from downregulation of energy metabolism pathways in EVs-RNA-seq.

claim: Various cell types in the brain may regulate RNA metabolism via the EVs pathway to resist hypoxic injury.
source: These results suggested that energy metabolism pathways in the brain may have been damaged by hypoxia, and various cell types in the brain may regulate RNA metabolism via the EVs pathway to resist hypoxic injury.
evidence: Inferred from upregulation of RNA metabolism pathways in EVs-RNA-seq.

claim: The function of mitochondria in the brain was severely impaired after hypoxia.
source: The Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA) showed that the function of mitochondria in the brain was also severely impaired after hypoxia (Figure 3—figure supplement 1I and J).
evidence: Supported by GSEA analysis of EVs-RNA-seq data.

claim: A significant increase in EVs secretion solely by brain endothelial cells was observed following hypoxia.
source: Our findings revealed the proportion of cells releasing EVs in each group, indicating a significant increase in EVs secretion solely by brain EC following hypoxia (Figure 3G, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: Supported by combined analysis of snRNA-seq and EVs-RNA-seq data in Figure 3G.

claim: Multiple differential mRNAs were present in EVs secreted by various types of cells after hypoxia, including mRNAs of hemoglobin subunits.
source: Multiple differential mRNAs were present in EVs secreted by various types of cells after hypoxia, including mRNAs of hemoglobin subunits, suggesting that this may be a common way for multiple cells to respond to hypoxia via the EVs pathway (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by combined analysis showing common mRNAs across cell types in Figure 3H.

claim: Exosomal mRNA levels of hemoglobin were significantly increased after hypoxia.
source: We therefore analyzed the hemoglobin mRNA levels in EVs from the two groups, and found that exosomal mRNA levels of hemoglobin were significantly increased after hypoxia, but only existed in EVs secreted by non-neuronal cells (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data of EVs in Figure 3I.

claim: Hemoglobin mRNA in EVs only existed in EVs secreted by non-neuronal cells after hypoxia.
source: We therefore analyzed the hemoglobin mRNA levels in EVs from the two groups, and found that exosomal mRNA levels of hemoglobin were significantly increased after hypoxia, but only existed in EVs secreted by non-neuronal cells (Figure 3I and J).
evidence: Supported by cell source analysis in Figure 3J showing absence in neuronal EVs.

claim: Changes in hemoglobin after hypoxia induction could be a common means by which various types of cells respond to hypoxia.
source: Many of these pathways were related to hemoglobin function, suggesting that changes in hemoglobin after hypoxia induction could be a common means by which various types of cells respond to hypoxia (Figure 3K).
evidence: Inferred from GO analysis showing hemoglobin-related pathways enriched across multiple cell types.

claim: Chronic hypoxia can enhance EVs communication in the brain.
source: Above all, chronic hypoxia can enhance EVs communication in the brain and induce non-neuronal cells to transcribe hemoglobin and release them in the form of EVs.
evidence: Summary statement based on EVs-RNA-seq findings showing increased EV secretion and hemoglobin mRNA.

claim: Chronic hypoxia induces non-neuronal cells to transcribe hemoglobin and release them in the form of EVs.
source: Above all, chronic hypoxia can enhance EVs communication in the brain and induce non-neuronal cells to transcribe hemoglobin and release them in the form of EVs.
evidence: Summary statement based on combined snRNA-seq and EVs-RNA-seq findings.

claim: Brain tissue in the H28d group remained red after perfusion with normal saline, indicating large amounts of hemoglobin in the brain.
source: We observed brain tissues from two groups of mice and found that brain tissue in the H28d group remained red after perfusion with normal saline, indicating large amounts of hemoglobin in the brain (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by visual observation of brain tissue in Figure 4A.

claim: The mRNA levels of hemoglobin subunits were low in all cell types in the control group.
source: We further explored the transcriptional changes in hemoglobin subunits in cells after hypoxia by snRNA-seq and visualized the results in a violin plot, and the mRNA levels of hemoglobin subunits were low in all cell types in the Con group, but were increased in non-neuronal cells after hypoxia (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by snRNA-seq data visualized in violin plot in Figure 4B.

claim: The mRNA levels of hemoglobin subunits were increased in non-neuronal cells after hypoxia.
source: We further explored the transcriptional changes in hemoglobin subunits in cells after hypoxia by snRNA-seq and visualized the results in a violin plot, and the mRNA levels of hemoglobin subunits were low in all cell types in the Con group, but were increased in non-neuronal cells after hypoxia (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by snRNA-seq data visualized in violin plot in Figure 4B.

claim: Hba-a1 mRNA levels in the brain were significantly increased after hypoxia.
source: RT-qPCR confirmed that Hba-al mRNA levels in the brain were significantly increased after hypoxia (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 4C.

claim: Hba protein levels were significantly increased in the H28d group.
source: Western blotting and immunofluorescence also revealed that Hba protein levels were also significantly increased in the H28d group (Figure 4D–G).
evidence: Supported by western blot and immunofluorescence data in Figure 4D-G.

claim: Transient hypoxia induced the expression of hemoglobin in neurons in the brain.
source: Although previous studies showed that transient hypoxia induced the expression of hemoglobin in neurons in the brain, its specific function is still unclear (Schelshorn et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schelshorn et al., 2009.

claim: The Hba fluorescence intensity in Map2-positive cells increased significantly after hypoxia.
source: We labeled Hba and Map2 by immunofluorescence and found that the Hba fluorescence intensity in Map2-positive cells increased significantly after hypoxia, indicating that hypoxia induced hemoglobin specifically expressed and accumulated in neurons (Figure 4H–J).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4H-J.

claim: Hypoxia induced hemoglobin specifically expressed and accumulated in neurons.
source: We labeled Hba and Map2 by immunofluorescence and found that the Hba fluorescence intensity in Map2-positive cells increased significantly after hypoxia, indicating that hypoxia induced hemoglobin specifically expressed and accumulated in neurons (Figure 4H–J).
evidence: Inferred from increased Hba fluorescence in Map2-positive neurons.

claim: Non-neuronal cells in the brain could dynamically regulate hemoglobin levels in neurons via the EVs pathway under hypoxia.
source: SnRNA-seq and EVs-RNA-seq showed that chronic hypoxia-induced hemoglobin transcription was mainly increased in non-neuronal cells and their secreted EVs (Figure 3J and Figure 4B), but immunofluorescence showed that hypoxia-induced increased hemoglobin was specifically present in neurons, confirming that non-neuronal cells in the brain could dynamically regulate hemoglobin levels in neurons via the EVs pathway under hypoxia, thus helping neurons to resist the hypoxic damage.
evidence: Inferred from combined snRNA-seq, EVs-RNA-seq, and immunofluorescence data showing hemoglobin transcription in non-neuronal cells but protein accumulation in neurons.

claim: Non-neuronal cells help neurons to resist hypoxic damage by regulating hemoglobin levels via the EVs pathway.
source: SnRNA-seq and EVs-RNA-seq showed that chronic hypoxia-induced hemoglobin transcription was mainly increased in non-neuronal cells and their secreted EVs (Figure 3J and Figure 4B), but immunofluorescence showed that hypoxia-induced increased hemoglobin was specifically present in neurons, confirming that non-neuronal cells in the brain could dynamically regulate hemoglobin levels in neurons via the EVs pathway under hypoxia, thus helping neurons to resist the hypoxic damage.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that hemoglobin is transferred from non-neuronal cells to neurons under hypoxia.

claim: Neuroglobin (Ngb) plays a crucial protective role in neural tissues during cerebral ischemia and hypoxia.
source: Neuroglobin (Ngb) is a recently discovered type of oxygen-carrying globin, which under hypoxic conditions can facilitate the diffusion of oxygen into mitochondria, enhancing tissue oxygen utilization. Particularly, it plays a crucial protective role in neural tissues during cerebral ischemia and hypoxia.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about neuroglobin function.

claim: Ngb transcription levels showed consistently low expression levels across various brain cell types before and after hypoxia.
source: To elucidate whether Ngb exerts protective effects in the brains of H28d mice, we conducted an analysis of snRNA-seq data. Visualization of Ngb transcription levels revealed consistently low expression levels across various brain cell types before and after hypoxia, contrasting with the behavior of hemoglobin.
evidence: Supported by analysis of snRNA-seq data.

claim: Mitochondrial complex I was significantly decreased in the brain after hypoxia.
source: Western blotting showed that mitochondrial complex I and IV were both significantly decreased in the brain after hypoxia, through analyzing the markers of mitochondrial complex I (NDUFB8) and complex IV (citrate synthase) (Figure 4K–M).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4K-M.

claim: Mitochondrial complex IV was significantly decreased in the brain after hypoxia.
source: Western blotting showed that mitochondrial complex I and IV were both significantly decreased in the brain after hypoxia, through analyzing the markers of mitochondrial complex I (NDUFB8) and complex IV (citrate synthase) (Figure 4K–M).
evidence: Supported by western blot data in Figure 4K-M.

claim: The activity of mitochondrial complex I was significantly decreased after hypoxia.
source: We further detected the activity of mitochondrial complex I in the brain in both groups and showed that its activity was significantly decreased after hypoxia (Figure 4N).
evidence: Supported by mitochondrial complex I activity assay in Figure 4N.

claim: Chronic hypoxia can damage mitochondrial activity in the brain.
source: These results confirm that chronic hypoxia can damage mitochondrial activity in the brain.
evidence: Inferred from decreased mitochondrial complex levels and activity.

claim: Hypoxia-induced non-neuronal transcriptionally increased hemoglobin is transmitted to neurons via the EVs pathway.
source: Above all, these results indicate that hypoxia-induced non-neuronal transcriptionally increased hemoglobin is transmitted to neurons via the EVs pathway.
evidence: Summary statement based on combined in vivo findings.

claim: The viability of hcMEC/D3 cells was significantly reduced in the H4h and subsequent groups, compared with the H0h group.
source: The viability of hcMEC/D3 cells was significantly reduced in the H4h and subsequent groups, compared with the H0h group, and the cytotoxicity was significantly increased in the H12h group (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by CCK-8 assay data in Figure 5A.

claim: The cytotoxicity of hcMEC/D3 cells was significantly increased in the H12h group.
source: The viability of hcMEC/D3 cells was significantly reduced in the H4h and subsequent groups, compared with the H0h group, and the cytotoxicity was significantly increased in the H12h group (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by LDH assay data in Figure 5B.

claim: The viability of SH-SY5Y cells was significantly reduced in the H4h and subsequent groups, compared with the H0h group.
source: The viability of SH-SY5Y cells was significantly reduced in the H4h and subsequent groups, compared with the H0h group, and the cytotoxicity was significantly increased in the H4h group and subsequent groups as well (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Supported by CCK-8 assay data in Figure 5C.

claim: The cytotoxicity of SH-SY5Y cells was significantly increased in the H4h group and subsequent groups.
source: The viability of SH-SY5Y cells was significantly reduced in the H4h and subsequent groups, compared with the H0h group, and the cytotoxicity was significantly increased in the H4h group and subsequent groups as well (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: Supported by LDH assay data in Figure 5D.

claim: Fluorescence intensity in SH-SY5Y cells decreased gradually with hypoxia time, indicating that the number of mitochondria was significantly reduced by prolongation of hypoxia.
source: Fluorescence intensity in SH-SY5Y cells decreased gradually with hypoxia time, indicating that the number of mitochondria was significantly reduced by prolongation of hypoxia (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by MitoTracker staining and flow cytometry data in Figure 5F.

claim: The mitochondrial membrane potential significantly decreased with prolongation of hypoxia in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: The mitochondrial membrane potential is an important indicator of mitochondrial function. Its reduction will induce mitochondrial homeostasis damage in cells, which in turn induces cell damage. We therefore evaluated the effects of hypoxia by JC-1 staining and found the mitochondrial membrane potential also significantly decreased with prolongation of hypoxia (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by JC-1 staining and flow cytometry data in Figure 5G.

claim: Severe mitochondrial damage occurred when neurons encountered hypoxic stress, which may be a key factor in hypoxic nerve injury.
source: These results indicate that severe mitochondrial damage occurred when neurons encountered hypoxic stress, which may be a key factor in hypoxic nerve injury.
evidence: Inferred from decreased mitochondrial number and membrane potential in neurons under hypoxia.

claim: The level of HBA1 mRNA was significantly upregulated in hcMEC/D3 cells in the H4h group, and then slowly decreased to pre-hypoxia levels.
source: The level of HBA1 mRNA was significantly upregulated in hcMEC/D3 cells in the H4h group, and then slowly decreased to pre-hypoxia levels (Figure 5H).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 5H.

claim: Level of HBA1 mRNA in SH-SY5Y cells was unaffected by hypoxia.
source: However, level of HBA1 mRNA in SH-SY5Y cells was unaffected by hypoxia (Figure 5I).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 5I.

claim: EVs were significantly increased in the H8h group compared with the H0h group, indicating that hypoxia for 8 h induced EVs release by hcMEC/D3 cells.
source: We then isolated and analyzed EVs from hcMEC/D3 cells under different treatment durations and showed that EVs were significantly increased in the H8h group compared with the H0h group, indicating that hypoxia for 8 h induced EVs release by hcMEC/D3 cells (Figure 5J, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by nanoparticle tracking analysis in Figure 5J.

claim: Hypoxia treatment for 8 h induced a significant transcription of hemoglobin in endothelial cells, which was subsequently released into the culture medium via EVs.
source: Above all, we established an experimental hypoxia method for EC and neurons in vitro, and found that hypoxia treatment for 8 h induced a significant transcription of hemoglobin in EC, which was subsequently released into the culture medium via EVs (Figure 5K).
evidence: Summary statement based on in vitro findings showing HBA1 transcription and EV release.

claim: hcMEC/D3 H8h EVs were actively taken up by SH-SY5Y cells.
source: The results showed that hcMEC/D3 H8h EVs were actively taken up by SH-SY5Y cells, thus providing a basis for subsequent exploration of the neuroprotective effect of EC-derived EVs (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy showing Dil-labeled EVs in SH-SY5Y cells in Figure 6A.

claim: EC-conditioned medium does not cause damage to the cell viability and mitochondrial homeostasis of SH-SY5Y cells.
source: We initially demonstrated that EC-conditioned medium does not cause damage to the cell viability and mitochondrial homeostasis of SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by safety detection data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: HBA1 mRNA levels were significantly upregulated in the H8h+H8h (EC) group.
source: HBA1 mRNA levels were significantly upregulated in the H8h+H8h (EC) group, suggesting that conditioned medium from EC treated with hypoxia for 8 h could increase the transcription of hemoglobin after hypoxia (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data in Figure 6B.

claim: Conditioned medium from endothelial cells treated with hypoxia for 8 h could increase the transcription of hemoglobin in neurons after hypoxia.
source: HBA1 mRNA levels were significantly upregulated in the H8h+H8h (EC) group, suggesting that conditioned medium from EC treated with hypoxia for 8 h could increase the transcription of hemoglobin after hypoxia (Figure 6B).
evidence: Inferred from increased HBA1 mRNA in neurons treated with EC-conditioned medium.

claim: Hba protein levels were significantly increased in the H8h+H8h (EC) group.
source: We also detected the protein levels of Hba by immunofluorescence and showed that Hba protein levels were significantly increased in the H8h+H8h (EC) group, confirming that H8h conditioned medium from EC could increase hemoglobin levels in neurons (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6C and D.

claim: H8h conditioned medium from endothelial cells could increase hemoglobin levels in neurons.
source: We also detected the protein levels of Hba by immunofluorescence and showed that Hba protein levels were significantly increased in the H8h+H8h (EC) group, confirming that H8h conditioned medium from EC could increase hemoglobin levels in neurons (Figure 6C and D).
evidence: Inferred from increased Hba protein in neurons treated with EC-conditioned medium.

claim: Treatment with H8h EC-conditioned medium improved the number of mitochondria in SH-SY5Y cells after hypoxia for 8 h.
source: Treatment with H8h EC-conditioned medium improved the number of mitochondria and mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 6F and G) and improved the viability of neurons after hypoxia for 8 h (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by MitoTracker staining data in Figure 6G.

claim: Treatment with H8h EC-conditioned medium improved mitochondrial membrane potential in SH-SY5Y cells after hypoxia for 8 h.
source: Treatment with H8h EC-conditioned medium improved the number of mitochondria and mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 6F and G) and improved the viability of neurons after hypoxia for 8 h (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by JC-1 staining data in Figure 6F.

claim: Treatment with H8h EC-conditioned medium improved the viability of neurons after hypoxia for 8 h.
source: Treatment with H8h EC-conditioned medium improved the number of mitochondria and mitochondrial membrane potential (Figure 6F and G) and improved the viability of neurons after hypoxia for 8 h (Figure 6H).
evidence: Supported by CCK-8 assay data in Figure 6H.

claim: hcMEC/D3 H8h EVs were actively taken up by primary neurons.
source: The results of immunofluorescence showed that hcMEC/D3 H8h EVs were actively taken up by PN (Figure 6I).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy showing Dil-labeled EVs in primary neurons in Figure 6I.

claim: The mRNA and protein levels of hemoglobin were significantly upregulated in primary neurons in the H8h+H8h (EC) group.
source: The PN were then subjected to EC-conditioned medium exchange combined with hypoxia treatment to determine if conditioned medium could increase the transcription and expression levels of hemoglobin. The mRNA and protein levels of hemoglobin were significantly upregulated in the H8h+H8h (EC) group (Figure 6J–L).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR and immunofluorescence data in Figure 6J-L.

claim: The mitochondrial membrane potential was significantly higher in primary neurons in the H8h+H8h (EC) group than in the H8h group.
source: JC-1 staining showed that the mitochondrial membrane potential was significantly higher in the H8h+H8h (EC) group than in the H8h group (Figure 6M).
evidence: Supported by JC-1 staining data in Figure 6M.

claim: Mitochondrial numbers were significantly increased in primary neurons in the H8h+H8h (EC) group compared with the H8h group.
source: MitoTracker staining showed that mitochondrial numbers were significantly increased in the H8h+H8h (EC) group compared with the H8h group (Figure 6N).
evidence: Supported by MitoTracker staining data in Figure 6N.

claim: Cell viability of primary neurons was significantly reduced after 8 h of hypoxia treatment, and this damage could be attenuated by EC-conditioned medium.
source: We also evaluated the viability of PN in each group by PI/Hoechst staining and showed that their cell viability was significantly reduced after 8 h of hypoxia treatment, and that this damage could be attenuated by EC-conditioned medium (Figure 6O).
evidence: Supported by PI/Hoechst staining data in Figure 6O.

claim: EC-derived EVs carrying hemoglobin mRNA could regulate hemoglobin levels in neurons under hypoxic conditions, aiding neurons in maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis and resisting hypoxic damage.
source: Above all, we found that EC-derived EVs carrying hemoglobin mRNA could regulate hemoglobin levels in neurons under hypoxic conditions, aiding neurons in maintaining mitochondrial homeostasis and resisting hypoxic damage (Figure 6P).
evidence: Summary statement based on in vitro findings with primary neurons.

claim: After removing EVs, the resulting conditioned medium failed to increase hemoglobin in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: After removing EVs, we verified that the resulting conditioned medium failed to increase hemoglobin in SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and the H8h EC-conditioned medium lost its abilities to improve mitochondrial homeostasis and neuronal viability under hypoxic stress (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The H8h EC-conditioned medium lost its abilities to improve mitochondrial homeostasis and neuronal viability under hypoxic stress after removing EVs.
source: After removing EVs, we verified that the resulting conditioned medium failed to increase hemoglobin in SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and the H8h EC-conditioned medium lost its abilities to improve mitochondrial homeostasis and neuronal viability under hypoxic stress (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7B-D showing loss of protective effects.

claim: Following HBA1 RNAi treatment of endothelial cells, the conditioned medium failed to increase hemoglobin in SH-SY5Y cells.
source: We screened plasmids for specific knock-down of HBA1 mRNA in hcMEC/D3 cells, and verified that the resulting conditioned medium failed to increase hemoglobin in SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D-F.

claim: Following HBA1 RNAi treatment of endothelial cells, the conditioned medium lost its abilities to improve mitochondrial homeostasis and neuronal viability under hypoxic stress.
source: Following HBA1 RNAi treatment of EC, the conditioned medium lost its abilities to improve mitochondrial homeostasis and neuronal viability under hypoxic stress (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: Supported by data in Figure 7F-H showing loss of protective effects.

claim: EVs containing hemoglobin mRNA secreted by endothelial cells after hypoxia treatment regulated the hemoglobin expression in neurons, thus helping neurons to resist mitochondrial dysfunction and nerve injury under hypoxia stress.
source: In summary, this study found that EVs containing hemoglobin mRNA secreted by EC after hypoxia treatment regulated the hemoglobin expression in neurons, thus helping neurons to resist mitochondrial dysfunction and nerve injury under hypoxia stress (Figure 7I).
evidence: Summary statement based on all in vitro findings including EV removal and RNAi experiments.

claim: Hypoxia enhances intercellular communication primarily through interactions involving EVs.
source: Mounting evidence suggests that hypoxia enhances intercellular communication primarily through interactions involving EVs, thereby facilitating the transmission of various cargoes with distinct functional roles (Korvenlaita et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to Korvenlaita et al., 2023 and Wang et al., 2023.

claim: Hypoxia induces a significant enhancement in EVs-mediated communication among various cell types in the brain.
source: Our research findings also indicate that hypoxia induces a significant enhancement in EVs-mediated communication among various cell types in the brain.
evidence: Supported by the study's own findings from combined snRNA-seq and EVs-RNA-seq analysis.
